extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary theory, philosophy of humor, and comedy scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Henri Bergson's criteria for what makes actions, characters, or situations comic — i.e., the philosophical/esthetic standards for recognizing and analyzing the comic. Useful for literary analysis, theory of humor, and comedic criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involuntary action / mechanical inelasticity
rubrics_metrics.description: They laugh because his sitting down is involuntary...the laughable element ... consists of a certain MECHANICAL INELASTICITY, just where one would expect to find the wide-awake adaptability and the living pliableness of a human being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a runner who stumbles because muscles continued the same movement when circumstances called for something else (stone on the road). Comic effect arises when an action that should be adaptable is instead rigid or automatic. Scoring/identification: prioritize whether the action is experienced/perceived as involuntary or as a failure of expected elasticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatism / machine-like continuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Habit has given the impulse: what was wanted was to check the movement or deflect it. He did nothing of the sort, but continued like a machine in the same straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: victim of a practical joke whose habitual movement yields absurd results (ink on pen, falling from a chair). Use this to identify comic instances where human behavior resembles mechanical repetition rather than responsive adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental (external) vs intrinsic (internal) comic
rubrics_metrics.description: All the same, in both cases the result has been brought about by an external circumstance. The comic is therefore accidental: it remains, so to speak, in superficial contact with the person. How is it to penetrate within? The necessary conditions will be fulfilled when mechanical rigidity no longer requires for its manifestation a stumbling-block ... but extracts by natural processes, from its own store, an inexhaustible series of opportunities for externally revealing its presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between superficial comic effects caused by external mishap and deeper comic dispositions that arise from the person's own internal rigidity. The latter produces more sustained and character-based comedy; classify examples accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absentmindedness / temporal lag of attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagine a mind always thinking of what it has just done and never of what it is doing, like a song which lags behind its accompaniment...to adapt ourselves to a past and therefore imaginary situation, when we ought to be shaping our conduct in accordance with the reality which is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an absent-minded person, someone reading romances who walks like a somnambulist (Don Quixote). Use this criterion to spot comic situations where behavior is governed by past or imaginary contexts rather than present reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived naturalness / traceability of cause increases comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When a certain comic effect has its origin in a certain cause, the more natural we regard the cause to be, the more comic shall we find the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: seeing absentmindedness develop before our eyes or knowing the origin of distraction (romances of love) makes the ensuing mishaps funnier. In analysis, give greater weight to comic effects whose cause is intelligible, plausible, or appears to arise 'naturally' from the character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic, organised absentmindedness and cumulative escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Their absentmindedness is systematic and organised around one central idea, and their mishaps are also quite coherent, thanks to the inexorable logic which reality applies to the correction of dreams, so that they kindle in those around them, by a series of cumulative effects, a hilarity capable of unlimited expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: over-romantic enthusiasts and Utopian dreamers whose consistent delusion produces a chain of related mishaps. Consider coherence and escalation: repeated, logically-connected blunders amplify comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vices as external rigidities (comic vice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The vice capable of making us comic is ... brought from without, like a ready-made frame into which we are to step. It lends us its own rigidity instead of borrowing from us our flexibility. We do not render it more complicated; on the contrary, it simplifies us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish vices that are incorporated and tragic from those that are externally appendaged and comic. Comic vices simplify and make the character resemble a puppet or frame; examples: stock comedic types (l'Avare, le Joueur).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of self / unconsciousness of the comic character
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic character is generally comic in proportion to his ignorance of himself. The comic person is unconscious...he becomes invisible to himself while remaining visible to all the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: characters who do not perceive the ridiculousness of their traits (contrast with tragic characters who are conscious). Use this to evaluate whether self-awareness diminishes comic effect (self-aware characters attempt to hide or modify defects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as a social corrective / social gesture
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter must be something of this kind, a sort of SOCIAL GESTURE. By the fear which it inspires, it restrains eccentricity, keeps constantly awake and in mutual contact certain activities ... and, in short, softens down whatever the surface of the social body may retain of mechanical inelasticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess comic moments for their social function: do they signal or regulate eccentricity/inelasticity? Recognize Bergson's normative claim that laughter serves to correct or discourage anti-social rigidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension and elasticity as healthy/adaptable norms; inelasticity as comic sign
rubrics_metrics.description: What life and society require of each of us is a constantly alert attention ... TENSION and ELASTICITY are two forces, mutually complementary ... If they are lacking in the mind, we find every degree of mental deficiency ... This rigidity is the comic, and laughter is its corrective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tension/elasticity as diagnostic criteria: lack of mental or character elasticity indicates comic potential. Differentiate pathological/inferior cases (sickness, insanity) from the more neutral zone where comic rigidity provokes laughter rather than material repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of incorporation of vice distinguishes comedy from drama
rubrics_metrics.description: A drama, even when portraying passions or vices that bear a name, so completely incorporates them in the person that their names are forgotten ... many comedies have a common noun as their title: l'Avare, le Joueur, etc. ... le Jaloux could only be the title of a comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this criterion when classifying works: if the vice remains an external, nameable principle (common-noun title), the work leans toward comedy; if the vice is integrated and personal, it tends toward drama.
